items: One of the world's earliest civilisations, the Elamites flourished in southwestern Iran for over two millennia.
Founded by Sargon of Akkad around 2334 BCE, the Akkadian Empire is widely regarded as history's first true empire.
The Third Dynasty of Ur (Ur III) was a Sumerian renaissance, with an elaborate bureaucratic state and monumental ziggurats including the great Ziggurat of Ur.
Tla2006 at English Wikipedia, Public domain
The Neo-Assyrian Empire became the most feared military power of its age, perfecting siege warfare and using terror as a deliberate tool of rule.
Under Hammurabi, Babylon became the leading power and cultural centre of Mesopotamia.
The Hittites were ancient Anatolia's dominant power and early workers of iron.
Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany, CC BY-SA 2.0
A powerful Hurrian kingdom that dominated northern Mesopotamia and Syria, the Mitanni were noted chariot warriors who established diplomatic marriages with Egypt's pharaohs.
Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0
The Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem, raised the Ishtar Gate and made Babylon one of antiquity's greatest cities.
Often called the first Iranian empire, the Medes joined forces with Babylon to sack Nineveh in 612 BCE and bring down Assyria.
Founded by Cyrus the Great, the Achaemenid Persian Empire was the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus.
The New Kingdom saw Egypt reach the height of its imperial power, with warrior pharaohs like Thutmose III and Ramesses II expanding into Nubia and the Levant.
The Kingdom of Kush outlasted Egypt's own empire, with its kings even ruling Egypt as the 25th Dynasty for nearly a century.
Carthage, founded by Phoenician settlers, became one of the ancient Mediterranean's greatest trading powers.
A Saharan empire that dug hundreds of underground channels (foggaras) to tap ancient groundwater, enabling agriculture in the heart of the desert.
The Fatimid Caliphate was an Ismaili Shia dynasty that ruled much of North Africa and founded Cairo as its capital.
A Berber Muslim dynasty that ruled North Africa and Iberia, the Almohads imposed a rigorous religious reform while their court patronised philosophers such as Averroes and Ibn Tufayl.
A Berber dynasty that arose from religious reformers in the Sahara, the Almoravids united the Maghreb and al-Andalus and checked the Christian advance at the Battle of Sagrajas in 1086.
Founded by one of Alexander's generals, the Ptolemaic dynasty made Alexandria the leading intellectual centre of the Hellenistic world.
One of antiquity's great trading powers, Aksum controlled the Red Sea trade routes and was among the first states to adopt Christianity.
Often regarded as the first great empire of West Africa, Ghana controlled the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade, becoming fabulously wealthy long before European contact with the region.
One of Africa's longest-lasting empires, Kanem-Bornu endured for around a thousand years through successive dynasties, controlling central Saharan trade routes from the Lake Chad basin.
The Ethiopian Empire traces its legendary origins to King Solomon, and its victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896 made it a symbol of African independence against colonialism.
The Mali Empire produced Mansa Musa, whose 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca was so laden with gold that his spending reportedly depressed the value of gold in Cairo for years.
The Kingdom of Benin in modern Nigeria produced the famous Benin Bronzes, among Africa's greatest artistic achievements.
The largest empire in West African history, Songhai ruled from its capital Gao, while Timbuktu flourished as a centre of trade and Islamic learning.
David Sessoms from Fribourg, Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0
The Oyo Empire was the dominant Yoruba state and one of West Africa's most powerful kingdoms, with a constitutional system that could depose an unpopular ruler.
The Jolof Empire united the Wolof peoples of Senegal in one of West Africa's early confederacies, controlling trade between the coast and the interior.
The Kingdom of Kongo was among Africa's most developed states, with a royal bureaucracy, written records after Portuguese contact, and diplomatic relations with the Vatican.
Ms. Milora Lipscomb, Mr. Bruce Mateso and Paari-editeur, CC BY-SA 2.5
Founded around 1430 by a prince linked to the declining Great Zimbabwe, the Mutapa Empire controlled the gold trade between the interior and coastal Swahili, and later Portuguese, merchants.
The Luba Empire in central Africa developed a system of sacred kingship and memory devices (lukasa boards) to record royal history and cosmology.
The Sultanate of Darfur was a powerful Islamic state in western Sudan that controlled trans-Saharan trade routes linking it to Egypt and North Africa.
The Ashanti Confederacy of Ghana was known for its wealth in gold and the sacred Golden Stool, symbol of the nation's soul.
Founded on the Zimbabwe plateau in the late 17th century, the Rozvi Empire carried on Great Zimbabwe's stone-building tradition and drove Portuguese traders from the interior.
Macvivo at English Wikipedia (Original text: Samwise Gamgee), CC BY-SA 3.0
The Lunda Empire of central Africa had a flexible political system that expanded by incorporating local rulers, spreading Lunda culture across a wide region.
Edited by J.F. Ade Ajayi (ed.)., CC BY-SA 4.0
The Sultanate of Adal waged a devastating jihad against Christian Ethiopia under Ahmad ibn Ibrahim and nearly destroyed the ancient Ethiopian Empire.
Rod Waddington from Kergunyah, Australia, CC BY-SA 2.0
The Empire of Kaabu began as Mali's western provinces and became a dominant Mandé state in West Africa, controlling coastal trade in modern Guinea-Bissau and Senegal.
The Sultanate of Wadai was a powerful Islamic state in the eastern Sahel, enriched by trans-Saharan trade, that resisted French conquest until its capital Abéché fell in 1909.
Founded by the reformer Usman dan Fodio, the Sokoto Caliphate was one of Africa's largest 19th-century states, a theocratic empire spanning much of modern Nigeria.
Alexander the Great's eleven-year campaign created one of the largest empires of antiquity and spread Greek culture from Egypt to India.
At its peak, the Roman Empire spanned some five million square kilometres and an estimated 50 to 70 million people.
Ángel M. Felicísimo from Mérida, España, Public domain
The Eastern Roman Empire survived nearly a thousand years after the fall of Rome in the West, preserving classical knowledge and Orthodox Christianity.
47-manasses-chronicle.jpg: Original: Constantine Manasses derivative work: Stegop, Public domain
Charlemagne's empire united much of Western Europe for the first time since Rome, launching the Carolingian Renaissance and laying the political foundations of modern France and Germany.
Charlemagne. Autorité émettrice de monnaie indéterminé. Atelier monétaire. Émetteur, Public domain
Voltaire quipped that it was 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire', yet this patchwork of mainly German states shaped central European politics for over eight centuries.
One of Europe's largest states and an early experiment in constitutional monarchy, the Commonwealth's noble democracy shaped Central European culture and politics.
Sweden's Age of Greatness saw this small Nordic kingdom become a major European power controlling much of the Baltic Sea, before overextension led to collapse at Poltava.
The largest empire in history, covering a quarter of the Earth's land surface, the British Empire shaped global trade, language, law, and culture.

France's imperial ambitions peaked first under Napoleon, who redrew the map of Europe, and again in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when France built the world's second-largest colonial empire.
Office of War Information, Overseas Picture Division. [1] The image prefix (LC-USW3) at the Library of Congress image..., Public domain
Often called the first global empire, Spain conquered the Aztec and Inca states and opened the Americas to European colonisation.
Portugal, a small kingdom of perhaps a million people, led Europe's Age of Discovery and built one of the first global maritime empires, with footholds from Brazil and West Africa to India and Japan.

In its 17th-century Golden Age this small republic became Europe's leading commercial power, and its East India Company (VOC), with permanent capital and tradable shares, is often called the first multinational corporation.
Michiel Jansz. van Mierevelt, Public domain
Begun in the 1880s with footholds in Eritrea and Somalia, Italy's colonial empire peaked under Mussolini, who dreamed of a new Roman Mediterranean.
The Dual Monarchy of 1867–1918 was one of Europe's most ethnically diverse states, home to a dozen or more nationalities.

Unified in 1871, the Kaiserreich industrialised so rapidly that it became continental Europe's leading industrial power, but its militarism, naval rivalry with Britain and anxious diplomacy helped bring on the First World War.
Spanning some 22.8 million square kilometres at its peak, the Russian Empire was one of the largest states in history, often ranked third after the British and Mongol empires.
Attributed to Jean-Marc Nattier, Public domain
Brazil's constitutional monarchy (1822–1889) was the only lasting empire in the Americas and one of 19th-century Latin America's most stable governments.
Mathew Benjamin Brady / Levin Corbin Handy, Public domain
Led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad, the Rashidun Caliphate (632–661) conquered Syria, Egypt, Iraq and the Sasanian Persian Empire in one of the fastest expansions in history.
Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyad Caliphate built one of the largest empires the world had yet seen, stretching from Spain to Central Asia and the Indus.
The Abbasid golden age brought major advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy, as scholars translated and built on Greek, Persian and Indian learning.
Abdulmomen Laith Mahmoud (عبدالمؤمن ليث محمود), CC BY-SA 4.0
Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187 and changed the balance of power in the medieval Middle East.
Ahmed Al.Badawy from Cairo, Egypt, CC BY-SA 2.0
The Mamluks, former slave soldiers, halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut in 1260 and went on to expel the last Crusaders from the Levant.
Five successive dynasties made the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) the dominant power of medieval North India.
The Seljuk Turks took Baghdad in 1055 as protectors of the Abbasid caliph and crushed the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071.
The Safavids made Twelver Shia Islam Persia's state religion from 1501, forging the Shia identity of modern Iran and a lasting sectarian rivalry with the Ottomans.
Nader Shah, sometimes called the Napoleon of Persia, briefly reunited Iran and campaigned from Delhi to the Caucasus.
The Zand dynasty under Karim Khan gave 18th-century Persia a rare period of relative stability, with Shiraz as its capital and a centre of the arts.
At their height the Mughals ruled most of the Indian subcontinent and had a syncretic culture.
Yann; edited by Jim Carter, CC BY-SA 4.0
The Ottoman Empire lasted over six centuries (c. 1299–1922) and at its height ruled across three continents.
The Mongol Ilkhanate ruled Persia and Mesopotamia, sacking Baghdad in 1258 before converting to Islam under Ghazan in 1295 and becoming a great patron of Persian art and scholarship.
The Khwarazmian Empire briefly dominated Central Asia before Genghis Khan's devastating invasion, one of history's most catastrophic conquests, largely triggered by Khwarazmian provocation.
The Xiongnu were the first great steppe empire to challenge China, raiding and extracting tribute from the Han for centuries.
The Han Dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) shaped Chinese civilisation for two millennia, and China's majority ethnic group still calls itself Han in its honour.

The Tang Dynasty is often considered China's golden age, when Chang'an, with perhaps a million inhabitants, was among the world's largest cities and a cosmopolitan centre of art, poetry and international trade.
The Song Dynasty introduced the first government-issued paper money, movable-type printing, gunpowder weapons and the magnetic compass at sea, and had one of China's most refined cultures.
The Ming Dynasty built the Forbidden City and the final Great Wall, restored Chinese sovereignty after Mongol rule, and launched Zheng He's naval expeditions.
The Manchu Qing was China's last imperial dynasty (1644–1912).
AnonymousUnknown author Qing Dynasty Court Painter, Public domain
Kublai Khan's Yuan Dynasty was the Chinese part of the Mongol Empire.
The Mongol Empire remains history's largest contiguous land empire.
The Chagatai Khanate, the Central Asian realm allotted to Genghis Khan's second son, Chagatai, ruled the lands between the Oxus and the Tarim Basin, gradually becoming Muslim and Turkic in culture.
Maître de la Mazarine, Public domain
Timur (Tamerlane) built his empire by devastating conquest, yet it became a centre of artistic refinement.
Gustavo Jeronimo from Aranjuez, Spain; derivative work by MrPanyGoff, CC BY 2.0
The First Turkic Khaganate made the Turkic peoples a major force in Eurasian history and was the first political entity to use the word 'Türk' as an identity.
Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0
The Khazar Khaganate, the steppe power between Byzantium and the Islamic caliphates, controlled the Volga trade route, and its ruling elite converted to Judaism.
The Tokugawa shoguns gave Japan over 250 years of internal peace (1603–1868) while tightly restricting foreign contact.
Imperial Japan's rapid modernisation after 1868 transformed a feudal, largely isolated state into a major industrial and military power within a single generation.
Under Ashoka the Great the Maurya Empire reached its peak and then changed course: Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga war, and his edicts and missions helped carry it beyond India.
आशीष भटनागर at Hindi Wikipedia, Public domain

The Gupta period is often called India's classical or golden age, when Aryabhata advanced astronomy and mathematics using the decimal place-value system and Kalidasa wrote his celebrated Sanskrit works.
Srivijaya was the dominant maritime power of Southeast Asia from the 7th to 13th centuries, controlling the Strait of Malacca and the sea trade between India and China.

The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat, the world's largest religious monument, in the middle of one of the pre-modern world's largest urban complexes, which a large network of reservoirs and canals sustained.
Majapahit was the high point of Hindu-Buddhist Java, a maritime power that claimed suzerainty over much of the modern Indonesian archipelago and remains a symbol of national unity.
The Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh was one of the last major powers to resist British expansion in India, known for its disciplined Khalsa army and religious tolerance.
The Parthian Empire held the Silk Road between Rome and China, grew rich as the middleman of Eurasian trade and resisted Roman conquest for centuries.
The last great pre-Islamic Persian empire, the Sasanians rivalled Rome and Byzantium for four centuries.
Founded by Seleucus, one of Alexander's generals, the Seleucid Empire spread Greek culture from Anatolia to Central Asia.
Rising from Shivaji's hill forts and guerrilla warfare, the Maratha Empire broke Mughal supremacy and dominated 18th-century India.
From their island capital Tenochtitlan, perhaps 200,000 strong and among the largest cities on earth in 1519, the Aztec Triple Alliance ruled much of central Mexico.
Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0
The largest city of the early Americas, whose avenues and pyramids in the Valley of Mexico shaped politics, trade and art across Mesoamerica.
The largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, Tawantinsuyu stretched some 4,000 km along the Andes, linked by roads and run without money or writing.
The Haudenosaunee league of five, later six, nations, bound by the Great Law of Peace and long the strongest Native power in north-eastern North America.
Spain’s richest viceroyalty, centred on Mexico City, which for three centuries governed Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and the Philippines.
France’s North American empire, stretching from the St Lawrence through the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico, and the origin of French-speaking Canada.
Spain’s great South American viceroyalty, ruled from Lima, whose silver from Potosí flowed across the world for nearly three centuries.
David Felipe Ruiz Hoyos, CC BY-SA 4.0
The Dutch plantation colony on the Guiana coast, notorious for harsh slavery and home to strong maroon nations, which became an independent republic in 1975.
A federal republic founded by thirteen British colonies in 1776 that grew across North America to become the world’s leading economic and military power.
The southern Haitian republic of Pétion and Boyer, which reunited Haiti, ruled all of Hispaniola for two decades and paid France a crushing indemnity.
The South American republic along the Pacific that became independent in 1818, known for long periods of constitutional stability, broken by the 1973 coup.
Bolívar’s great republic uniting Venezuela, New Granada, Quito and Panama, which won independence for northern South America but broke apart in 1830.
Luis Enrique Toro Moreno (1897-1933), Public domain
The Andean republic that grew from the heart of the Inca Empire and Spain’s richest viceroyalty, declared independent in 1821.
The exact author is disputed. Some sources attribute it to Jean Baptiste Madou, others to the art teacher of San Martin's …, Public domain
Federation of the five former provinces of the Kingdom of Guatemala, a liberal experiment that collapsed in civil war after less than two decades.
The landlocked Andean republic named after Simón Bolívar, born from Upper Peru in 1825 and refounded as a plurinational state in 2009.
The South American republic that left Gran Colombia in 1830 and, transformed by the world’s largest oil reserves, became Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian Republic.
Andean republic on the equator, independent of Gran Colombia since 1830, shaped by Quito–Guayaquil rivalry, export booms and the Galápagos Islands.
Central American republic since 1838, coveted for its canal route and shaped by William Walker, US occupation, the Somoza dynasty and the Sandinistas.
Central American republic since 1838, the original ‘banana republic’, shaped by American fruit companies, military rule and Cold War politics.
The smallest and most densely populated country of mainland Central America, independent since 1841, shaped by coffee, military rule and civil war.
Central America’s most populous state, a republic since 1847, marked by coffee dictatorships, the CIA-backed coup of 1954 and a long civil war.
Republic reunited under Buenos Aires in 1861 that became one of the world’s richest countries by 1914 before a century of coups and crises.
The Mexican republic since the defeat of Maximilian in 1867, shaped by the Porfiriato, the Revolution of 1910 and seven decades of one-party rule.
A federation founded in 1867 from British colonies that grew into the world’s second-largest country and a parliamentary democracy under the Crown.
A federation of six former British colonies founded in 1901, now a parliamentary democracy and middle power spanning an entire continent.
Isthmian republic created in 1903 with US backing to build the Panama Canal, which it finally took full control of in 1999.
Independent island nation since 1947, known for its welfare state, nuclear-free policy, radical 1980s reforms and Treaty of Waitangi settlements.
Photographer unidentified. Retouched by TimofKingsland., Public domain
The first Chinese dynasty attested by its own writing, whose oracle bones, bronzes and royal tombs at Anyang open the recorded history of China.
The great eastern state of ancient China, home of the first hegemon Duke Huan, the reformer Guan Zhong and the Jixia Academy, and the last to fall to Qin.
Confucius and his disciples,, Public domain
The dynasty that overthrew the Shang, proclaimed the Mandate of Heaven and ruled northern China through kinsmen planted in regional states.
The vast southern kingdom of the middle Yangtze, whose distinctive culture produced the Songs of Chu and which was Qin's strongest rival.
The western frontier state that turned itself into a war machine through Shang Yang's reforms and conquered all its rivals to unify China in 221 BCE.
Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the eastern steppe, famed for gold-rich kurgans, who later carved out kingdoms in Bactria, Sistan and north-western India.
Nomads of the Gansu corridor who, driven west by the Xiongnu, conquered Bactria and gave rise to the Kushan Empire.
The nomadic confederation that replaced the Xiongnu on the Mongolian steppe, whose clans later founded the Northern Wei and other dynasties of northern China.
The longest-lived of Korea's Three Kingdoms, which unified most of the peninsula in the 7th century and built a Buddhist golden age at Gyeongju.
The largest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, a fortress-based warrior state that ruled Manchuria and the northern peninsula and repelled Sui and Tang invasions.
A south-western Korean kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period, famed for refined Buddhist art and for passing writing, Buddhism and crafts to Japan.
An empire of Yuezhi origin stretching from the Amu Darya to the Ganges, a crossroads of Rome, China and India that carried Buddhism into Central Asia.
The Jin dynasty in exile at Jiankang, where northern aristocrats preserved Chinese court culture and turned back the Former Qin at the Fei River in 383.
The steppe empire that dominated Mongolia between the Xianbei and the Turks, and whose rulers made khagan the title of supreme steppe rule.
The empire of the Yarlung kings that united the Tibetan plateau, rivalled Tang China for the Silk Road and brought Buddhism and writing to Tibet.
A kingdom of Manchuria and northern Korea founded by Goguryeo and Mohe people, so prosperous that Tang China called it the flourishing land of the east.
The first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam as a state religion, which brought Transoxiana under Turkic rule and produced classic works of Turkic literature.
A dynasty from the mountains of Ghor in central Afghanistan that built the Minaret of Jam and laid the foundations of Muslim rule in northern India.
The empire of the Khitan people, which ruled Mongolia, Manchuria and the far north of China for two centuries and gave China its medieval name, Cathay.
The Korean dynasty that reunified the peninsula in 936, gave Korea its Western name and produced inlaid celadon, the Tripitaka Koreana and early metal type.
A Turkic dynasty from Ghazni whose sultan Mahmud raided deep into India and whose court patronised Persian literature, including Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.
The empire of the Jurchen people, who overthrew the Khitan Liao, drove the Song from northern China and ruled it until the Mongol conquest of 1234.
The Mongol khanate of the western steppe that ruled the Rus' principalities for over two centuries and grew rich on trade from its capital, Sarai.
Korea's last and longest-ruling dynasty, which made Neo-Confucianism the basis of state and society and created the Hangul alphabet.
Sejong the Great of Joseon, Public domain
The island kingdom of Okinawa, ruled from Shuri, that grew rich as a trading hub between China, Japan and Southeast Asia until Japan annexed it.
The nomadic khanate of the Kazakh steppe, founded by Kerei and Janibek around 1465, which gave the Kazakhs their name, law and homeland.
The last great nomadic empire of the steppe, an Oirat Mongol state that fought the Qing for Central Asia until its destruction in the 1750s.
The republic that ended imperial rule in China in 1912 and, after losing the mainland in 1949, continued on Taiwan as a prosperous democracy.
上海波尔照相馆, Public domain
The Communist state proclaimed by Mao Zedong in 1949, which has governed mainland China ever since and grown into the world’s second-largest economy.
Reunited Egypt of the Eleventh to Thirteenth Dynasties, famed for its literature, its Nubian fortresses and the reclamation of the Faiyum.
Markh at English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0
The united Berber kingdom of Masinissa and Jugurtha, Rome's powerful ally and then enemy in North Africa.
Credits to Zakaria Mimouni / Wikimedia Commons Algerian Wikimedians User Group, CC BY-SA 4.0
Rome's richest African province, centred on rebuilt Carthage, the granary of Rome and a heartland of Latin Christianity.
Egypt as the richest province of the Roman and Byzantine empires, the granary of Rome and a birthplace of Christian monasticism.
The Christian Nubian kingdom of Dongola that halted the Arab advance up the Nile and flourished for some seven centuries.
The Berber dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya from Tunis for over three centuries, a Mediterranean trading power that claimed the Almohad caliphate’s mantle.
The Sultanate of Sennar, which replaced Christian Alodia and ruled the middle Nile for three centuries, spreading Islam across Sudan.
The sharifian dynasty that drove the Portuguese from much of Morocco, defeated them at the Battle of the Three Kings and conquered Songhai.
The Ottoman corsair state of Algiers, governed by pashas, aghas and finally deys, a major Mediterranean naval power for three centuries.
France’s largest settler colony, conquered from 1830 and governed as part of France, whose end in 1962 came after one of the bloodiest wars of decolonisation.
Ionian port city of the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders, and later the chief city of Roman Asia.
Rich Ionian island state famed for its wine and mastic, a leading naval power of the Aegean and home of the Homeridae, who claimed descent from Homer.
The greatest Ionian city, mother of dozens of colonies around the Black Sea and birthplace of Greek natural philosophy with Thales and Anaximander.
Ionian island state that under the tyrant Polycrates became the leading naval power of the Aegean and built the famous Tunnel of Eupalinos.
Militarised city-state of Laconia with two kings and a helot workforce, the dominant land power of Classical Greece and victor over Athens in 404 BCE.
City-state of Attica that created democracy, led the Delian League and produced the drama, philosophy and architecture central to Classical Greek culture.
Leading city-state of Iron Age Crete on the site of the great Minoan palace, rival of Gortyn until the Roman conquest of 67 BCE.
Sanctuary-state of Apollo on Mount Parnassus, whose oracle was consulted for centuries by Greek cities and foreign kings.
Megarian colony on the Bosporus that controlled the passage to the Black Sea and later became Constantinople.
Celtic-speaking peoples of the central Iberian plateau whose long resistance to Rome ended with the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE.
Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
The Roman state from the expulsion of the kings to Augustus, which grew from a city in Latium to master of the Mediterranean before collapsing in civil war.
The strongest Thracian state, a kingdom stretching from the Aegean to the Danube whose rich tombs and Greek-style city of Seuthopolis survive in Bulgaria.
Long-lived Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait that fed Athens with Black Sea grain and survived as a Roman client state until the coming of the Huns.
Island republic created in 408 BCE that became the leading Hellenistic naval and commercial power of the eastern Mediterranean, home of the Colossus.
gravure sur bois de Sidney Barclay numérisée Google, Public domain
Macedonian kingdom of Antigonus I's heirs, who dominated Greece from Pella with phalanx and fortresses until Rome defeated Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE.
Iranian-speaking horse nomads who displaced the Scythians, held the steppe from the Volga to the Danube and fought Rome with armoured lancers.
Federation of Peloponnesian cities that under Aratus and Philopoemen united the whole Peloponnese, until Rome destroyed it and sacked Corinth in 146 BCE.
Roman province of western Iberia, roughly modern Portugal and Extremadura, governed for four centuries from the veteran colony of Emerita Augusta.
The largest Roman province in Hispania, from the Pyrenees to Galicia, governed from Tarraco until the Visigoths ended Roman rule in Iberia in the 470s.
The Roman province of Britannia (43–c. 410), which brought towns, roads, villas, Latin and Christianity to most of what is now England and Wales.
A confederation of Germanic peoples on the upper Rhine and Danube that overran Rome’s Agri Decumates and gave its name to Germany in French and Spanish.
A confederation of Germanic peoples on the lower Rhine whose kings conquered Gaul and founded the realm from which France and Germany both grew.
A confederation of north German peoples who raided Roman coasts, settled England and fought Charlemagne for thirty years before forced conversion.
Early medieval kingdom of northern and eastern Scotland, known for its carved symbol stones, which merged with the Gaels to form the kingdom of Alba.
Catfish Jim and the soapdish, CC BY-SA 3.0
Kingdom of mid and north-east Wales and the Marches that long faced Mercia across Offa’s Dyke, until it split into two lordships after 1160.
The most enduring Welsh kingdom, ruled from Aberffraw on Anglesey, whose princes led Welsh resistance until Edward I’s conquest in 1283.
The Frankish realm founded by Clovis, the most lasting of the barbarian kingdoms and the common ancestor of France and Germany.
A Gaelic kingdom spanning north-east Ireland and Argyll whose kings, settling Scotland’s west coast, helped make Gaelic the language of medieval Scotland.
The kingdom of the West Saxons, which survived the Viking onslaught under Alfred the Great and grew into the Kingdom of England.
Gregory the Great, unknown writer, Public domain
The great midland kingdom that dominated England in the 8th century under Aethelbald and Offa, whose Dyke still marks the Welsh border.
One of Germany's oldest territories, a duchy for more than a thousand years under the Agilolfings, Welfs and Wittelsbachs, and the core of modern Bavaria.
Steppe empire centred on the Carpathian basin that dominated central Europe's Slavs, besieged Constantinople and lasted until Charlemagne broke it.
The kingdom of the Angles north of the Humber, home of Bede, Lindisfarne and the Northumbrian Renaissance, later carved up by the Vikings.
Medieval Bulgarian state founded by Asparuh's Bulgars, which adopted Christianity, nurtured Slavonic literature and rivalled Byzantium for three centuries.
The ‘Most Serene Republic’, a merchant state on the lagoon that ruled a maritime empire across the Adriatic and Aegean for a thousand years.
A Muslim Bulgar state on the middle Volga that grew rich on the fur trade and was the northernmost outpost of Islam for three centuries.
The first Christian kingdom in Iberia after the Muslim conquest, born at Covadonga and seen as the starting point of the Reconquista.
The lands of central Italy ruled by the popes as temporal sovereigns for over a thousand years, from Pepin’s donation to the capture of Rome in 1870.
The original uploader was Snowdog at Italian Wikipedia., CC BY-SA 3.0
The independent Umayyad state in al-Andalus founded by a refugee prince in 756, which built the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
Great principality of southern France, heart of Occitan culture and troubadour poetry, destroyed by the Albigensian Crusade.
The Basque Pyrenean kingdom of Pamplona, which under Sancho III dominated Christian Spain and kept its own laws until 1841.
José Luis Filpo Cabana, CC BY-SA 4.0
The medieval and early modern kingdom of the Scots, forged from Pictland and Dál Riata, independent until the Union with England in 1707.
The stem duchy of northern Germany whose dukes became kings and emperors, later the power base of Henry the Lion before its break-up in 1180.
Rich medieval county on the North Sea whose cloth towns of Bruges, Ghent and Ypres made it one of the wealthiest regions of Europe.
Jan van Eyck / Presumably Hubert van Eyck, Public domain
One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, united in the Viking Age, joined to Denmark and Sweden for five centuries and independent again since 1905.
The first great East Slavic state, ruled by the Rurikid princes from Kiev, which brought Orthodox Christianity to the lands of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.
The great duchy of south-western France, home of troubadour courts and Eleanor of Aquitaine, fought over by the kings of England and France for three centuries.
A county of the southern Low Countries ruled from Mons for nine centuries, rich in cloth and coal and long linked by marriage to Flanders and Holland.
The Christian kingdom that succeeded Asturias in 910, claimed Visigothic heritage and in 1188 held one of Europe's first parliaments with townsmen.
José Luis Filpo Cabana, CC BY 3.0
The Viking settlement on the lower Seine that became one of Europe’s best-run principalities and launched the Norman conquest of England.
The wine-rich duchy around Dijon, home of Cîteaux and the Capetian dukes, that under its Valois dukes became the seed of a great European power.
The kingdom unified by Æthelstan in 927 that developed the common law and Parliament, was reshaped by the Norman Conquest and joined Scotland in 1707.

The civilisation of the Maya peoples of southern Mexico and northern Central America, whose kingdoms, temple cities, writing and calendars flourished for over two thousand years before the Spanish conquest.

The maize-farming peoples of the Mississippi valley and the American South-East, c. 800–1600, whose chiefs ruled from towns of earthen platform mounds around plazas, Cahokia the greatest of them.

The Late Bronze Age civilisation of mainland Greece, named after Mycenae, whose palace states wrote the earliest known Greek in Linear B, built massive citadels and tombs, and lived on in the memory of Homer’s epics.

A farming culture of central Nigeria, c. 1500 BCE to the turn of the Common Era, whose hollow terracotta figures are among the earliest sculpture known south of the Sahara and whose people smelted iron early.

The earliest major civilisation of Mesoamerica, which flourished in the Gulf Coast lowlands of Mexico c. 1200–400 BCE and is known for its colossal stone heads, jade carving and early images of rulers and gods.

The seafaring people of Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and their sister cities on the Lebanese coast, who founded Carthage and colonies across the Mediterranean and spread the alphabet from which Greek and Latin descend.

Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the Eurasian steppe, famed as mounted archers, whose kings ruled north of the Black Sea from the 7th to the 3rd century BCE and were buried in great mounds rich in gold.

An Iranian people of Central Asia, centred on Samarkand and Bukhara, whose merchants dominated the Silk Road trade with China from the 4th to the 8th century and whose alphabet lives on in the Mongolian script.

Seafaring Scandinavians who from the late 8th to the 11th century raided, traded and settled from Newfoundland to the Caspian Sea, founding towns and states and leaving their mark on the languages and lands of Europe.

The movement to end the Atlantic slave trade and slavery, pressed by campaigners, preachers, writers and the enslaved themselves, which between 1787 and 1888 ended legal slavery throughout the Americas.

The struggle inside South Africa and across the world against apartheid, the system of racial segregation and white minority rule imposed from 1948, which ended with the first democratic election in 1994.

The movement in the United States, led chiefly by African Americans in the South, whose lawsuits and non-violent protests ended legal segregation and won federal protection of voting rights between 1954 and 1968.

A movement of ideas in 17th- and 18th-century Europe and its colonies that championed reason, science, toleration and reform, and whose thinkers shaped modern ideas of rights, government and knowledge.

The struggle against British rule in India, from the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885 to independence and partition in 1947, waged through petitions, mass non-violent campaigns and armed revolt.

The organised effort of wage-earners, through trade unions, cooperatives and parties of their own, to win better pay, shorter hours, safer work and a voice in politics, born with industry around 1800.

The movement of scholars and teachers, begun by Petrarch’s generation in 14th-century Italy, that recovered the literature of Greek and Roman antiquity and made the humanities the core of European education.

A movement in literature, art, music and thought that spread across Europe and the Americas from the 1790s, prizing feeling, imagination, nature, the individual and the national past over the rules of reason.

The transformation of the study of nature in early modern Europe, from Copernicus to Newton, that replaced the Earth-centred cosmos and Aristotle’s physics with a mathematical and experimental science.
The century-long campaign, from the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 to the Swiss vote of 1971, that won women the right to vote and to stand for election in most of the world’s states.

The devotional movement that began among Tamil poet-saints around the 6th century and spread across India over a thousand years, teaching love of a personal god in songs in the people’s own languages.

The Arab cultural renaissance of the 19th century, centred in Cairo and Beirut, in which writers, translators and teachers renewed the Arabic language and literature through printing, the press and new schools.

A programme of reform in Qing China from 1861 to 1895, led by court ministers and provincial governors, that adopted Western weapons, ships and industry to save the dynasty while keeping the Confucian order.

Rule by a hereditary monarch who holds supreme power unchecked by any constitution, parliament or court: the form claimed by the great monarchies of early modern Europe and kept by a handful of states today.
Rule by a small privileged class claiming to be the best fitted to govern, in practice usually a hereditary nobility, from the early Greek city-states to the upper houses of Europe’s monarchies.

A chiefdom unites several villages under a hereditary paramount chief who rules through kinship, ritual and tribute rather than officials, a form that governed peoples from ancient Mesopotamia to Hawaii and Africa.

A city-state is a single city that governs itself and its surrounding countryside; from Sumer, Greece and Phoenicia to Venice and the Hanseatic towns it nurtured citizenship, trade and republican government.

Colonial rule is government of a territory and its people by a distant state that treats them as subjects rather than citizens; from 1415 to the 20th century it carried European power across most of the world.

A monarchy in which the sovereign reigns under a constitution while elected parliaments and ministers govern: the form of most surviving monarchies, from the United Kingdom and Spain to Japan and Thailand.

Rule by one leader or a small group holding near-absolute power, unchecked by law or free elections: named after the Roman Republic’s emergency magistrate, it became the modern name for unaccountable rule.

Government in which the citizens themselves decide laws and policies, in an open assembly or by popular vote, instead of through elected representatives: practised in classical Athens and in Switzerland today.

A monarchy in which the ruler is chosen by election rather than by birth, by princes, nobles, councils or fellow rulers: the form of the Holy Roman Empire and Poland–Lithuania, and of the papacy and Malaysia today.

A state whose constitution divides power between a central government and self-governing member states, neither able to abolish the other: pioneered by the United States in 1789, now home to some 40 per cent of humanity.

Feudalism was the medieval European order in which lords granted fiefs to vassals for military service and loyalty, leaving public power divided among landholders; historians now debate whether the term fits.

Government by a council of military officers, usually installed by a coup and ruling by decree in the name of order or national salvation; common after 1945, above all in Latin America, Africa and Asia.

A nomadic confederation joins herding tribes under one ruling clan and its khan; from the Xiongnu to the Mongols such steppe powers built the largest land empires and drew tribute from China and Constantinople.

Rule by a few, usually the rich or well-born, in their own interest: the constitution of many Greek cities and of merchant republics such as Venice, and today a loose term for the political power of great wealth.
A state in which one political party holds a legal or practical monopoly of power and others are banned or kept subordinate: the form of communist, fascist and many post-colonial regimes since 1918.

Democracy in which the government is formed from an elected parliament and stays in office only while it keeps parliament’s confidence: born in 18th-century Britain, now the usual form in Europe and the Commonwealth.

Democracy in which a separately elected president heads the government for a fixed term and cannot be dismissed by the legislature, under a constitution that divides and balances powers: devised in the United States.

Government without a monarch, in which the state is the public’s affair, run by elected magistrates and councils under law: born in ancient Rome, revived in medieval Italy and the Netherlands, now the usual form.

Government in the name of God or the gods, by priests, a sacred ruler or religious law; the word was coined for ancient Judea, and the Papal States, Tibet under the Dalai Lamas and Iran are classic examples.
One-man rule seized outside the traditional order of a Greek city-state, common from the 7th century BCE, whose name Plato and Aristotle turned into the West’s word for cruel and lawless power.

The Bell Beaker culture, c. 2800–1800 BCE, is an archaeologists’ name for a phenomenon of western and central Europe marked by bell-shaped beakers, copper daggers and archery gear, spread by trade and, in places, large migrations.

The Caral–Supe civilisation, also called Norte Chico, built platform mounds and sunken plazas in the river valleys of Peru’s north-central coast from c. 3000 to 1800 BCE and is the oldest known civilisation of the Americas.

The Đông Sơn culture was a Bronze Age culture centred on the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam (c. 1000 BCE – 1st century CE), famed for bronze drums that are found across Southeast Asia and southern China.

The Hopewell tradition was a network of Native American peoples of the Eastern Woodlands, from about 100 BCE to 500 CE, linked by long-distance exchange and known for geometric earthworks, burial mounds and fine carved pipes.

The Igbo-Ukwu culture of south-eastern Nigeria, known from a shrine, a burial and a cache first dated to the 9th century CE, cast the region’s earliest known bronzes and traded for beads from beyond the Sahara.
The hunter-gatherer and early farming culture of the Japanese archipelago from c. 14,000 to 300 BCE, known for cord-marked pottery among the oldest in the world, settled villages and dogū figurines.

The Kerma culture, or Kingdom of Kerma, was a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan from about 2500 to 1500 BCE that grew to rival Egypt, raided deep into it and left a great mudbrick temple and royal tumuli.

The last Neolithic jade culture of the Yangtze River Delta in China, c. 3300–2300 BCE, whose walled city at Liangzhu near Hangzhou, with its palace complex and flood defences, is perhaps among East Asia’s earliest state societies.

The Māori are the Indigenous Polynesian people of New Zealand (Aotearoa), whose ancestors arrived by canoe around 1300 and built a culture of iwi and hapū, carving, pounamu and pā long before the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840.

Mehrgarh, near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, Pakistan, is one of the earliest known farming and herding sites in South Asia, lived in from a Neolithic village (c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE) until about 2600–2000 BCE.

The Mumun culture of the Korean Peninsula (c. 1500–300 BCE), named by archaeologists after its plain pottery, saw the rise of intensive farming, large villages and the first chiefdom-like societies in Korea.

The Natufian culture of the Levant, c. 13,000–9,500 BCE, was a culture of hunter-gatherers who lived in settled villages before farming began and who may be the ancestors of the region’s first Neolithic builders.

The Nazca culture flourished on the desert coast of southern Peru from about 100 BCE to 800 CE, painting polychrome pottery, weaving fine textiles and making the Nazca Lines and the underground aqueducts called puquios.

The Oxus civilisation, or Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, was a Bronze Age urban culture of southern Central Asia (c. 2300–1700 BCE), known for walled towns such as Gonur Depe, fine metalwork and wide trade.

The Painted Grey Ware culture, named by archaeologists after its fine grey pottery painted in black, was an Iron Age culture of the western Gangetic plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley in northern India, c. 1200–600 BCE.

The Sámi are the Indigenous people of Sápmi, in the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, present there since the Bronze Age or early Iron Age and known for their Uralic languages, reindeer herding and joik.

Sangam-age Tamilakam was the ancient Tamil country of southern India, c. 300 BCE–300 CE, ruled by the Chera, Chola and Pandya dynasties and known above all from the classical Tamil poems of the Sangam corpus.

A Bronze Age culture of Sichuan in south-west China, contemporary with the Shang dynasty, known from the sacrificial pits at Sanxingdui near Guanghan with their bronze masks, gold and jade in a style new to Chinese art.

South India’s megalithic culture, an archaeologists’ name for its Iron Age burials in stone cists, stone circles and clay urns, is known from sites such as Brahmagiri and Adichanallur, c. 1200 BCE–300 CE.

The Taíno were the Indigenous farming peoples of the Greater Antilles, the Bahamas and the northern Lesser Antilles, ruled by caciques; the first people Columbus met in 1492, they live on in their descendants today.
The Thracians were Indo-European-speaking peoples of south-eastern Europe, known from Homer to the 6th century CE for their horsemen and peltasts, gold and silver treasures and the Odrysian Kingdom.

The Thule, or proto-Inuit, were Arctic whale hunters who arose in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and spread east across northern Canada to Greenland by the 13th century, becoming the ancestors of all Inuit and Yupik peoples.

The Vedic civilisation of the northern Indian subcontinent, c. 1500–500 BCE, composed the Vedas, whose rituals, gods and social order became one of the main foundations of later Hindu traditions.

The Yamnaya culture was a herding culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, c. 3300–2600 BCE, known for burial mounds and wagons and widely linked with the spread of Indo-European languages and ‘steppe ancestry’.

A Neolithic farming culture of the middle Yellow River in China, c. 5000–3000 BCE, known for millet farming, ditch-enclosed villages such as Banpo and painted pottery with fish, face and geometric designs.

The wet-rice farming culture that spread through the Japanese archipelago from northern Kyushu between about 300 BCE and 300 CE, bringing bronze and iron, permanent villages and the first polities named in Chinese records.

The parliamentary republic that replaced communist rule in Hungary in 1989, remembered for its peaceful change of system, its entry into NATO and the European Union, and the democratic backsliding of the Orbán era.

The West German state formed in 1949 from the three western occupation zones, which absorbed the German Democratic Republic in 1990 and became Europe's largest economy and a leading member of the European Union.

The parliamentary democracy restored in Greece after the fall of the military junta in 1974, remembered for the Metapolitefsi, European Communities membership from 1981 and the debt crisis of 2010 to 2018.

The Second Austrian Republic, re-established in 1945 after seven years inside Nazi Germany, remembered for a decade of Allied occupation, the State Treaty and perpetual neutrality of 1955 and its prosperity within the European Union.

The nation state proclaimed in 1923 on the Anatolian core of the Ottoman Empire after the War of Independence, remembered for Atatürk's secular reforms, NATO membership and its turn to a presidential system in 2017.

The kingdom Abdulaziz Ibn Saud united from Nejd, the Hejaz and eastern Arabia in 1932, an absolute monarchy allied with Wahhabi clerics, remembered as the world's leading oil exporter and guardian of Mecca and Medina.

The republic proclaimed in 1926 and independent from 1943, governed by a confessional pact among its religious communities, remembered for Beirut's golden age, the civil war of 1975–1990 and its collapse after 2019.
The republic resumed when Syria left the United Arab Republic in 1961, ruled by the Ba'ath from 1963 and the Assads from 1970 until Damascus fell in 2024, remembered for its civil war and refugees.

The Republic of Azerbaijan, independent since 1991 on the western Caspian shore, is an oil- and gas-exporting Turkic state remembered for the Nagorno-Karabakh wars with Armenia and the rule of the Aliyev family.

The Republic of Armenia, independent since 1991 in the highlands of the South Caucasus, is a landlocked Christian nation shaped by the Nagorno-Karabakh wars, blockaded borders, a large diaspora and the 'velvet revolution' of 2018.

Georgia, independent since April 1991, is a Black Sea republic shaped by the secessionist wars in Abkhazia and South Ossetia, the Rose Revolution, the Russian invasion of 2008 and a disputed turn away from Europe.

The Republic of Uzbekistan, independent since 1991, is Central Asia's most populous state, a doubly landlocked producer of cotton, gold and gas ruled for 25 years by Islam Karimov and reformed under Shavkat Mirziyoyev.

The Republic of Egypt, proclaimed in 1953 after the Free Officers' coup, is the most populous Arab state, shaped by Nasser's pan-Arabism, four wars with Israel, peace in 1979 and military rule since 2013.
The Kingdom of Morocco, ruled by the Alawi dynasty since Mohammed V became king in 1957 after independence from France and Spain, is a North African middle power marked by the Western Sahara dispute.

The Islamic Republic of Pakistan, proclaimed in 1956, is a nuclear-armed South Asian state of 241 million people, shaped by wars with India over Kashmir, the secession of Bangladesh and alternating military and civilian rule.

The Republic of Singapore, independent since its expulsion from Malaysia in 1965, is an island city-state that rose without natural resources to the world's highest GDP per head under the People's Action Party.

A Himalayan Buddhist monarchy under the Wangchuck dynasty since 1907, a British and then Indian protectorate in foreign affairs until 2011, which became a constitutional democracy in 2008.

The first new sovereign state of the 21st century, a Catholic, Portuguese- and Tetun-speaking republic on the eastern half of Timor, born in 2002 from Portuguese rule, Indonesian occupation and genocide, and a UN-run transition.

A small, densely peopled East African republic, independent from Belgium in 1962, whose Hutu-led governments ended in the 1994 genocide of the Tutsi, rebuilt since by the Rwandan Patriotic Front as an authoritarian, fast-growing state.

The republic restored in 1859 after Soulouque's empire, heir of the only state born of a slave revolt, marked since by debt to France, US occupation, the Duvalier dictatorship and today's collapse of the state.
A republic born in 1828 as a buffer between Argentina and Brazil, torn by civil wars in its first century, then a pioneering welfare state and today one of the world's most stable democracies.
A Mediterranean city-state ruled by the House of Grimaldi since 1297, a vassal and protectorate of France, which turned a casino and the absence of income tax into the wealthiest place on earth.

The Tangut empire of the Hexi Corridor that held the Silk Road against Song, Liao and Jin for two centuries, created its own script and pioneered movable type, until the Mongols annihilated it in 1227.

The Tuoba Xianbei dynasty that unified northern China in 439, carved the Yungang and Longmen grottoes and, through Empress Dowager Feng's reforms and Emperor Xiaowen's sinicisation, laid the foundations of the Sui and Tang.
The first imperial dynasty of China, which unified the Warring States in 221 BCE under Qin Shi Huang, standardised the realm's writing, coinage and measures, and collapsed fourteen years later.

The steppe confederation of the Huns, who drove the Goths into the Roman Empire from 370, extorted gold from Constantinople and under Attila invaded Gaul and Italy before breaking up after his death in 453.

The empire of the Hephthalites or White Huns, based in Tokharistan, which killed the Sasanian king Peroz I in 484, took tribute from Persia, ruled Sogdia and the Tarim Basin, and fell to the Turks and Sasanians around 560.

A Turkic steppe empire of the Toquz Oghuz tribes that replaced the Göktürks in Mongolia, saved the Tang from the An Lushan rebellion at a price in silk, and adopted Manichaeism before the Kyrgyz destroyed it.

The Western Liao, a Central Asian empire founded by Khitan refugees from the Jin conquest under Yelü Dashi, which crushed the Seljuks at Qatwan in 1141 and ruled Muslim vassals from Balasagun until the Mongols.
The Afghan empire founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747, which conquered Punjab, Kashmir and Khorasan, crushed the Marathas at Panipat, and is counted the founding state of modern Afghanistan.
The short-lived dynasty that reunified China in 589 after centuries of division, built the Grand Canal and laid the institutional foundations of the Tang before collapsing in revolt.

The puppet state Japan set up in occupied Manchuria in 1932 under the last Qing emperor Puyi, an industrial base built on slave labour and terror that served the invasion of China until the Soviet army destroyed it in 1945.

A Sumerian city-state near the ancient mouth of the Euphrates and seat of the moon god Nanna, remembered for the treasures of its Royal Cemetery and as the city from which Ur-Nammu's Third Dynasty came to rule Mesopotamia.

A Sumerian city-state of Lagash, Girsu and Nina on the lower Mesopotamian plain, whose rulers Eannatum and Gudea left the Stele of the Vultures, the Gudea cylinders and the earliest known reforms of Urukagina.
A Phoenician port with two harbours on the Lebanese coast, famed for its glass and purple dye, mother city of Tyre by its own claim, and under Persian rule the paramount city of Phoenicia.

An Iron Age kingdom of west-central Anatolia centred on Gordium on the Sangarius, which under King Midas dominated most of the peninsula and rivalled Assyria until the Cimmerians destroyed its capital.

The Hellenistic kingdom of Greater Armenia founded by Artaxias I after the Seleucid defeat at Magnesia, which under Tigranes the Great briefly ruled from the Caucasus to Syria before becoming a client state of Rome.

The Georgian polity of Egrisi on the eastern Black Sea, known to the Greeks as Colchis, land of Medea and the Golden Fleece, rich in gold, iron, timber and honey, and reckoned the earliest Georgian state.
The first great age of pharaonic Egypt, from the Third to the Sixth Dynasty, when god-kings ruling from Memphis raised the Step Pyramid and the pyramids of Giza and sent ships to Lebanon and Punt.

Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel on a mountain ridge above the Urubamba River in southern Peru, believed to have been a royal estate of the emperor Pachacuti and one of the major archaeological sites of the Americas.

The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum on the Yamuna at Agra, India, commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and regarded as one of the best examples of Mughal architecture.

Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865) was the 16th president of the United States, who led the Union through the American Civil War from 1861, issued the Emancipation Proclamation and was assassinated in Washington in 1865.

Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, was king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE, who conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and led his army as far as northwestern India.

Ashoka (c. 304 – 232 BCE) was the third ruler of the Maurya Empire, Emperor of Magadha from c. 268 BCE, who conquered Kalinga and then propagated dhamma through edicts inscribed across the Indian subcontinent, and patronised Buddhism.

Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator (69–30 BCE) was Queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt from 51 BCE and its last active ruler, who allied herself with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony and died as Octavian made Egypt a Roman province.

Confucius (c. 551 – c. 479 BCE), born Kong Qiu, was a Chinese philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period in the state of Lu, whose teachings on morality, family and government became Confucianism.

Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600 – 530 BCE), known as Cyrus the Great, founded the Achaemenid Empire by conquering Media, Lydia and Babylon, and is remembered for a policy of tolerance towards the customs and religions of conquered peoples.

Elizabeth I, the last monarch of the House of Tudor, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603; her reign saw an English Protestant church established, the Spanish Armada defeated and a flowering of English drama.
Genghis Khan (born Temüjin; c. 1162 – 1227) was the founder and first khan of the Mongol Empire, who united the Mongol tribes by 1206 and then conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) was an Arab scholar, historian and judge, born in Tunis, who served rulers across North Africa and in Granada and wrote the Muqaddimah, an introduction to history regarded as a forerunner of sociology and economics.

Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author who conquered Gaul, defeated his rival Pompey in a civil war and ruled the Roman Republic as dictator from 49 BCE until his assassination in 44 BCE.

Kamehameha I, also known as Kamehameha the Great, was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who conquered the Hawaiian Islands, completed their unification in 1810 and ruled as the first king of the Kingdom of Hawaii until his death in 1819.

Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci was an Italian painter, draughtsman, engineer and scientist of the High Renaissance, who worked in Florence, Milan, Rome and France and is remembered for the Mona Lisa, The Last Supper and his notebooks.

Mansa Musa (c. 1280 – c. 1337) was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire in West Africa, remembered for his wealth in gold, his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and Timbuktu's growth as a centre of Islamic learning.

Napoleon Bonaparte was a Corsican-born general of the French Revolution who became First Consul in 1799 and was Emperor of the French from 1804 to 1814 and again in 1815, leading campaigns across Europe and enacting lasting legal reforms.

Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013) was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison, negotiated the end of apartheid and served from 1994 to 1999 as the country's first black president.

Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (c. 1137 – 1193), known as Saladin, was a Sunni ruler of Kurdish origin who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, became the first sultan of Egypt and Syria, and took Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

Simón Bolívar (1783–1830) was a Venezuelan military officer and statesman, known as El Libertador, who led what are now Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru and Venezuela to independence from the Spanish Empire.

Wu Zetian (624–705), personal name Wu Zhao, was empress consort and empress dowager of the Tang dynasty and, from 690 to 705, emperor of her own Zhou dynasty, the only undisputed female sovereign in the history of China.

Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath, born in Stagira, who founded the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum in Athens and whose works contain the earliest known systematic study of logic.
Charlemagne (748–814) was King of the Franks from 768, King of the Lombards from 774 and emperor from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was crowned in Rome by Pope Leo III.

Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) was a French peasant's daughter who, claiming divine guidance, helped raise the siege of Orléans and secure the coronation of Charles VII during the Hundred Years' War, and was burned for heresy at Rouen.

Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German priest, theologian and former Augustinian friar whose Ninety-five Theses of 1517 made him the seminal figure of the Protestant Reformation and whose theological beliefs form the basis of Lutheranism.

Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was an English mathematician, physicist and polymath whose Principia of 1687 set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who also worked on optics and calculus and served as Master of the Royal Mint.

Catherine II, born the German princess Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729, overthrew her husband Peter III in 1762 and ruled Russia as empress until 1796, expanding the empire and presiding over the Russian Enlightenment.
Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng or Zhao Zheng in 259 BCE, was the king of Qin who conquered the other warring states by 221 BCE, founded the Qin dynasty and became the first emperor of China.

Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, became Great Khan of the Mongols in 1260, founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and by 1279 completed the conquest of the Song, becoming the first non-Han emperor of all China.

Tokugawa Ieyasu, born Matsudaira Takechiyo in 1543, was a Japanese daimyo who seized power after the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan from 1603 until 1868.
Hammurabi was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon, reigning from c. 1792 to c. 1750 BCE, who brought almost all of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule and issued the law code that bears his name.

Ramesses II, known as Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty; he reigned for 66 years from 1279 BCE and is remembered for the Battle of Kadesh, a peace treaty with the Hittites and his monuments.
Suleiman I, known as Suleiman the Magnificent, was the Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign of conquest, lawmaking and building is regarded as the peak of the Ottoman Empire's power.

Harun al-Rashid was the fifth Abbasid caliph, who reigned from 786 to 809; his reign is traditionally regarded as the beginning of the Islamic Golden Age and is remembered through the One Thousand and One Nights.

Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Balkhī, known as Rumi, was a thirteenth-century Persian-language Sufi mystic and poet who lived in Konya in Anatolia; he is remembered for the Masnavi and as the figure from whom the Mevlevi Order descends.

Hannibal was a Carthaginian general and statesman who commanded Carthage's forces against the Roman Republic in the Second Punic War, crossed the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE and destroyed a Roman army at Cannae before his defeat at Zama.

Haile Selassie I, born Tafari Makonnen, was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974, remembered for his appeal to the League of Nations against the Italian invasion, his reforms, and his place in Rastafari.

Toussaint Louverture was a Haitian general, born into slavery in French Saint-Domingue, who became the most prominent leader of the Haitian Revolution and governor-general for life before dying a prisoner in France in 1803.

George Washington was a Virginia planter who commanded the Continental Army in the American Revolutionary War, presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and served as the first president of the United States from 1789 to 1797.

Liliʻuokalani was the only queen regnant and last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ruling from 1891 until her overthrow in 1893, and the composer of "Aloha ʻOe" and author of a memoir of her country.

The feudal military government of Japan during the Muromachi period, ruled by the Ashikaga clan from Kyoto, remembered for arts shaped by Zen Buddhism, Noh theatre and its slide into the Sengoku wars.
A Mughal province in North India that its nawabs turned into an independent kingdom, then a British protectorate, until the East India Company annexed it in 1856.
The Tamil empire of the Imperial Cholas, founded by Vijayalaya in 848 in the Kaveri valley, which under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I ruled southern India and raided Srivijaya across the sea.

Company rule in India was the government of the British East India Company over much of the Indian subcontinent from the Battle of Plassey in 1757 until the Crown took over after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
A semi-autonomous Kingdom of Poland created by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 in personal union with the Russian Empire, stripped of its autonomy after the uprisings of 1830 and 1863.
A confederacy of between 150 and 330 Greek city-states under Athenian hegemony, founded in 478 BCE to continue the war against Persia, which became the naval empire known as the Athenian Empire.
The duchy formed in 1525 when the Teutonic Order's Prussian lands were secularised under Albert as a Polish fief; the first Protestant state, it passed to Brandenburg and became a kingdom in 1701.
The Islamic state of Sicily, conquered from the Byzantine Empire by the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya and later ruled by the Kalbid emirs, a prosperous Mediterranean power with Palermo as its capital.

The largest state of the Weimar Republic, a parliamentary democracy governed mostly by Social Democrats, deposed by the Prussian coup of 1932, absorbed by the Nazi regime and abolished by the Allies in 1947.
The parliamentary republic that governed France from 1870 to 1940, the longest-lasting French system of government since 1789, which built a vast colonial empire and won the First World War.

A Hellenistic Greek kingdom in Central Asia founded by the Seleucid satrap Diodotus I, remembered for its cities such as Ai-Khanoum, its coinage and its spread of Greek culture towards India and China.
A late medieval sultanate of western India, ruled by the Muzaffarid dynasty from Ahmedabad, remembered for its trade, its navy at Diu and its Indo-Islamic architecture until Akbar annexed it in 1573.
A Second World War Axis puppet state ruled by Ante Pavelić's fascist Ustaše in occupied Yugoslavia from 1941 to 1945, which carried out a genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma.
The first feudal military government of Japan, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo at Kamakura and later run by the Hōjō regents, remembered for repelling the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281.
A Tatar successor state of the Golden Horde on the Middle Volga, ruled from Kazan over the former lands of Volga Bulgaria until the Tsardom of Russia conquered it in 1552.
The Kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia in union with Hungary from Coloman's coronation at Biograd in 1102 until Louis II's death at Mohács in 1526, keeping its own Sabor, ban and nobility.
A monarchy under the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen dynasty from 1881 to 1947, which doubled in size after the First World War as Greater Romania and ended with the abdication of King Michael I.
A Balkan monarchy proclaimed in 1882 that doubled its lands in the Balkan Wars, was overrun in World War I and merged in 1918 into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.
A feudal Crusader state founded by the leaders of the Fourth Crusade on Byzantine lands after the sack of Constantinople in 1204, it held the city until the Nicaean recovery of 1261.
The first of the four Southern dynasties of China, founded by the general Liu Yu at Jiankang, remembered for the prosperous Reign of Yuanjia, its wars with Northern Wei and its violent court.

The independent Lithuanian republic declared on 16 February 1918, governed from Kaunas while Poland held Vilnius, authoritarian under Antanas Smetona from 1926, and occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940.
A province of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, formed from Teutonic Order lands in 1466, self-governing until 1569 and annexed by the Kingdom of Prussia in the partitions of Poland.
A medieval Eastern Orthodox empire proclaimed by Stefan Dušan in 1346, which stretched from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth and broke apart after the death of Stefan Uroš V in 1371.
The second period of the Song dynasty, ruled from Lin'an (now Hangzhou) after the Jin conquest of the north, remembered for its maritime trade, paper money, first permanent navy and Neo-Confucianism.
Thebes was the leading polis of the Boeotian League in central Greece, remembered for Epaminondas's victory over Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE and its destruction by Alexander the Great in 335 BCE.

Tibet was a de facto independent state ruled by the Ganden Phodrang government of the Dalai Lamas from the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912 until its annexation by the People's Republic of China in 1951.

The French State, the authoritarian rump state headed by Marshal Philippe Pétain from 1940 to 1944 after the German victory in the Battle of France, which collaborated with Nazi Germany, including in the deportation of Jews.
Germany's first constitutional republic, from 9 November 1918 to 23 March 1933, remembered for hyperinflation, the Golden Twenties and its collapse into Adolf Hitler's dictatorship.
Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and known as Octavian, was the founder of the Roman Empire and its first emperor from 27 BCE to 14 CE, whose principate opened the era of the Pax Romana.
Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, a Persian philosopher and physician of the Islamic Golden Age who served Iranian courts and wrote The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing.

Babur (1483-1530), born Zahīr ud-Dīn Muhammad, was a Timurid prince of Fergana who lost his Central Asian lands, ruled Kabul and in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire in northern India; he is also remembered for his memoir, the Baburnama.

Charles Darwin, an English naturalist and geologist whose voyage on HMS Beagle and decades of research led to On the Origin of Species (1859) and the theory that species descend from common ancestors through natural selection.

Frederick II, King in Prussia and later King of Prussia from 1740 to 1786, who seized Silesia, held it through the Seven Years' War, took part in the First Partition of Poland and patronised the Enlightenment.
