Hatshepsut was the sixth pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt, ruling from c. 1479 to c. 1458 BCE first as regent and then as queen regnant, and is remembered for her trade expeditions and building works.

José Rizal (1861-1896) was a Filipino ophthalmologist, writer and reformer of the late Spanish colonial period whose novels Noli Me Tángere and El filibusterismo shaped Filipino nationalism; executed by Spain in 1896, he is popularly…

Justinian I, called Justinian the Great, was Roman emperor at Constantinople from 527 to 565, remembered for reconquering North Africa and Italy, codifying Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis and rebuilding the Hagia Sophia.

Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher, the last of the Five Good Emperors, whose reign saw the Parthian and Marcomannic wars and the Antonine Plague and who wrote the Meditations.

Nzinga Mbande (c. 1583 – 1663), called Ngola Njinga by her people, was queen of the Ambundu kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day Angola, remembered for decades of war and diplomacy against Portuguese expansion.

Peter I (1672–1725), known as the Great, was tsar of all Russia from 1682 and its first emperor from 1721, remembered for the Great Northern War, the founding of Saint Petersburg and sweeping Westernizing reforms.

Sejong (1397–1450), known as Sejong the Great, was the fourth king of Joseon, reigning from 1418 to 1450, remembered above all for the creation of Hangul and for a reign of advances in science, medicine and agriculture.
Shaka kaSenzangakhona (c. 1787 – 1828) was king of the Zulu Kingdom from 1816 to 1828, remembered for reorganising the Zulu army and for wars whose part in the Mfecane remains disputed.

Shivaji I (c. 1630-1680), of the Bhonsle family, turned his father's jagir near Pune into the Maratha Kingdom, fought the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire with hill forts and guerrilla tactics, and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674.

Sun Yat-sen (1866-1925) was a Chinese physician and revolutionary who led anti-Qing movements from exile, became first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912 and founded the Kuomintang's political creed, the Three…

Sundiata Keita (c. 1217 – c. 1255) was a Mandinka prince who defeated Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso at Kirina and founded the Mali Empire, remembered above all through the Epic of Sundiata kept by the griots.

Timur, or Tamerlane, a Turco-Mongol conqueror of the Barlas tribe who founded the Timurid Empire in the late 14th century, campaigning from Delhi to Anatolia with great slaughter while patronising scholars and building up Samarkand.

Zheng He, born Ma He, was a Chinese admiral and diplomat of the early Ming dynasty, a eunuch in the service of the Yongle Emperor, who commanded seven treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433.

The Aeneid is a Latin epic poem by Virgil, written between 29 and 19 BCE, telling how the Trojan Aeneas fled Troy and reached Italy to become ancestor of the Romans; it became central to Latin education.

The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex in Granada, begun in 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, and the only well-preserved palace of the medieval Islamic world.

An embroidered cloth nearly 70 metres long, probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux and made in England in the decades after 1066, telling the story of the Norman conquest and the Battle of Hastings.

Beowulf is an anonymous Old English epic of 3,182 alliterative lines, set in 5th- and 6th-century Scandinavia and preserved in a single manuscript of about 975–1025, one of the most important works of Old English literature.

The Book of the Dead is an ancient Egyptian funerary text of magic spells, written mostly on papyrus from the beginning of the New Kingdom to around 50 BCE, meant to guide the dead through the underworld into the afterlife.

Chichen Itza is a large pre-Columbian Maya city in Yucatán, Mexico, a regional capital of the northern Maya lowlands from about 600 to 1100, known for the Temple of Kukulcán, the Great Ball Court and the Sacred Cenote.

The Colosseum is the elliptical amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, begun under Vespasian in 72 and completed under Titus in 80, the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built and a lasting symbol of Imperial Rome.

Ancient Jewish manuscripts of the Second Temple period, dated from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE and found in caves near Qumran between 1946 and 1956, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical books.

Domesday Book is the manuscript record of the Great Survey of much of England and parts of Wales, ordered by William the Conqueror and traditionally dated to 1086, and a primary source for English economic history.
The Forbidden City is the imperial palace complex in the centre of Beijing, built from 1406 to 1420 under the Yongle Emperor and home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors until 1924, now the Palace Museum.

The Great Sphinx of Giza is a limestone statue of a resting sphinx carved from the bedrock of the Giza Plateau, probably under Khufu or Khafre in the Old Kingdom, and the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt.

Great Zimbabwe is the stone-walled city near Masvingo built by ancestral Shona people from the 11th to the 15th century, capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe and the largest of the many 'houses of stone' of southern Africa.
A royal charter of rights sealed by King John of England at Runnymede in 1215 to make peace with rebel barons; reissued many times, it later became a symbol of liberty and the rule of law.

The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic attributed to Homer, composed around the 8th or 7th century BCE, which follows Odysseus's ten-year journey home from the Trojan War and stands among the oldest works of literature still read.

The Pantheon is a Roman temple in Rome, first built by Marcus Agrippa under Augustus and rebuilt under Hadrian, probably dedicated about 126; a church since 609, its dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

Petra is the rock-cut city in southern Jordan that the Nabataeans settled in the 4th century BCE and made their capital, a trading hub on the incense routes known for its carved sandstone façades and water systems.

The Ramayana is a Sanskrit epic of ancient India, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, which tells the life and journey of Rama, prince of Ayodhya, and has shaped Hindu life and the arts of South and Southeast Asia.
A granodiorite stele inscribed in 196 BCE with a decree of Egyptian priests for King Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, whose three versions became the key to deciphering Egyptian writing.

A prehistoric megalithic monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, built in phases from about 3100 BCE to about 1600 BCE by a people without writing, and aligned on the solstice sunrise and sunset.

The Tao Te Ching, or Laozi, is an ancient Chinese classic traditionally attributed to the sage Laozi and compiled during the Warring States period, the foundational text of Taoism and one of the most translated works in the world.

The Apache are Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the American Southwest, the Southern Plains and Northern Mexico, who call themselves Indé, resisted Spanish, Mexican and American invasion for centuries and live today in…

The Chamorro, or CHamoru, are the Indigenous people of the Mariana Islands in Micronesia, seafarers who arrived about 1,500 BCE, built on latte stones, and today live on Guam, the Northern Marianas and across the United States.

The Cimmerians were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people of the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes who crossed the Caucasus in the 8th century BCE and shook Urartu, Phrygia, Lydia and the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

The Corded Ware culture was a broad archaeological horizon of northern, central and eastern Europe between about 2900 and 2300 BCE, named for its cord-impressed pottery and thought a likely vector of Indo-European languages.

The Cycladic culture was a Bronze Age culture of the Cyclades in the Aegean Sea, c. 3100–1000 BCE, best known for its schematic white marble figurines and for the seafaring that linked its small island communities.
The Garamantes were an ancient people of the Fezzan in southern Libya who, from at least 1000 BCE to the late 7th century CE, built a desert kingdom on qanat irrigation and trans-Saharan trade.

The Guaraní are culturally related Indigenous peoples of South America, distinguished by the Guarani language, whose traditional range lies in Paraguay, Misiones, southern Brazil, Uruguay and Bolivia, and who number around 280,000 today.

The Haudenosaunee, "those who build the longhouse", also called the Iroquois or Six Nations, are a confederacy of Iroquoian peoples of northeast North America, united under the Great Law of Peace and still governed by their Grand Council.

The Jurchens were Tungusic-speaking peoples of Manchuria, first recorded in 748, who founded the Jin dynasty (1115–1234) and, under Nurhaci, the Later Jin, before Hong Taiji renamed them Manchus in 1635.

The Linear Pottery culture (LBK) was a Neolithic archaeological horizon of central Europe, c. 5500–4500 BCE, whose farmers spread agriculture along the Danube, Elbe and Rhine and built the largest free-standing buildings of their time,…

The Nubians are a people indigenous to Nubia, the Nile valley from southern Egypt to northern Sudan, who speak Nubian languages, built the kingdoms of Kush and Christian Nubia, and live today in Egypt and Sudan.
The Picts were a group of peoples in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth in the Early Middle Ages, remembered for their carved symbol stones, their silverwork and the kingdom of Fortriu.

Tartessos was a civilisation of the southern Iberian Peninsula, from the late Bronze Age to the 5th century BCE, rich in metals, trading with Phoenicians and Greeks, and writing in the Southwest script.

The Tlingit, or Lingít, are an Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, Alaska Natives and First Nations in Canada, known for their matrilineal clans, crest art and a hunting, fishing and gathering life built on rich fisheries.

The Vinča culture was a Neolithic culture of the central Balkans, 5400–4500 BCE, known for some of the largest settlements of prehistoric Europe, dark-burnished pottery, figurines, the Vinča symbols and the earliest known copper smelting.
The Zapotec civilisation flourished in the Valley of Oaxaca in Mesoamerica from about 700 BCE to 1521 CE, with Monte Albán, one of the first major cities of Mesoamerica, as the centre of its state.

The Soviet republic of Armenia, with its capital at Yerevan, created by the Sovietisation of the First Republic in 1920, which grew from an agricultural hinterland into an industrial centre and became independent in 1991.
The communist state proclaimed by Hồ Chí Minh in Hanoi in 1945, which defeated France at Điện Biên Phủ, ruled the North after the partition of 1954 and conquered the South in 1975.
An Iron Age kingdom in the south of present-day Jordan, east of the Arabah, remembered for its copper mines, its god Qaus and its long rivalry with Israel and Judah in the Hebrew Bible.

The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the federation of Serbia and Montenegro formed in 1992 after the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, remembered for sanctions, hyperinflation and the Kosovo War.

The Spanish State ruled by Francisco Franco, first in the Nationalist-held territories during the Spanish Civil War and then over all Spain until his death in 1975, a single-party dictatorship of National Catholicism and repression.

The republic founded in 1792 during the French Revolution, which abolished the monarchy, executed Louis XVI, passed through the Reign of Terror, the Directory and the Consulate, and ended with Napoleon's empire in 1804.

The German colony of the African Great Lakes region, taking in present-day mainland Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, remembered for the violence of its conquest, the Maji Maji Rebellion and Lettow-Vorbeck's wartime campaign.

The Kingdom of Cambodia of 1953–1970, the Sangkum period, was Norodom Sihanouk's first administration, from independence from France to the coup of 1970, remembered for his one-party rule and his neutrality in the Vietnam War.
A kingdom of the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, formed in the partition of 910 and later joined to León and Castile, centred on the pilgrim city of Santiago de Compostela and dissolved in 1833.
The kingdom without a king that the Regent Miklós Horthy ruled from 1920 to 1946, shaped by the losses of the Treaty of Trianon, which joined the Axis and took part in the Holocaust.

Korea as a colony of the Empire of Japan under the name Chōsen, ruled by a Governor-General in Keijō from the annexation of 1910 until Japan's surrender in 1945, and remembered for forced assimilation, extraction and mass mobilisation.

The Marcomanni were a Suebian Germanic people beside the Roman Danube frontier, recorded from 58 BCE to about 400 CE, remembered for the Bohemian kingdom of Maroboduus and the Marcomannic Wars against Marcus Aurelius.

The British protectorate north of the Zambezi, ruled by the British South Africa Company until 1924 and then by the Crown, whose Copperbelt mines made it rich and which became independent as Zambia in 1964.

The Pechenegs were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who controlled much of the steppes of southeast Europe and the Crimean Peninsula in the 9th and 10th centuries, raiding Kievan Rus' and serving Byzantium.
Portugal's colony on the Atlantic coast of west-central Africa, founded at Luanda in 1575, for two centuries a great slave-trading enterprise tied to Brazil, and independent as Angola in 1975.

The anti-communist state of southern Vietnam, proclaimed by Ngô Đình Diệm in 1955 after the partition at the 17th parallel, which fought the Vietnam War with American support until the fall of Saigon in 1975.

The Polish state reborn at the end of the First World War after more than a century of partitions, which won the Polish–Soviet War, fell under Piłsudski's Sanacja regime and was destroyed by the German and Soviet invasions of 1939.
The democratic republic that governed Spain from the deposition of King Alfonso XIII in 1931 until its defeat by the Nationalist rebels of General Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War in 1939.

The southern branch of the Xiongnu, formed when eight tribes broke from the chanyu Punu in 48 and settled inside Han China's northern frontier as tributary auxiliaries until Cao Cao ended the chanyu's court.
